title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday—One Size Fits Most
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: This installment of The Beacon, the Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning newsletter, acknowledges the difficulty of writing for a PK-12 faculty and offers a deliberately broad set of resources, each paired with a concrete try-this suggestion. It points teachers to Edutopia's learning-science video collection, recommending the warm demander clip as a move for any grade. It highlights Andrew Watson's review of a meta-analysis on mini-whiteboards and draws out the general principle that students do better when everyone responds frequently, proposing that teachers replace single raised hands with all-at-once responses. It then features Christopher Burn's account of surveying and interviewing primary pupils about a new feedback policy, connecting it to the CTL's own student advisory board and suggesting teachers solicit student views on one small aspect of their practice. The issue closes with an exchange from Austin Kleon's typewriter interview with George Saunders about teaching and staying in touch with something ageless. The throughline is practical, low-cost adjustments that work across divisions.
points: The editors borrow Frances Hesselbein's line that you have to carry a big basket to take something home to frame a cross-division resource list.
Mini-whiteboards are valued less as a tool than as a forcing function that makes every student respond and exposes misconceptions mid-lesson.
Teachers are urged to replace one-raised-hand questioning with whole-class simultaneous responses to remove the free rider problem.
Student feedback is recommended in small doses: ask about one specific practice, such as rubrics, and change one thing in response.
quotes: Given the complexity of teaching and learning, there is no one-size-fits-all approach that can meet the needs of teachers across divisions and disciplines
Pull the “Warm Demander” video from the elementary collection and notice one moment this week where you could pair a clear expectation with visible warmth.

the forcing function of requiring all students to respond, and being able to see their responses relatively easily, adds a layer of formative assessment that allows a teacher to respond to any misconceptions amidst instructional intervals.
Doing so eliminates a potential free rider problem in your classroom, activates all students thinking, and doesn’t let opting out become a default response.
If we want students to take ownership of their learning, then it’s helpful for them to actually have some.

engage students with questions about one specific aspect of your teaching (think small: something like rubrics, grading policies, or your own feedback structures) and change one small thing based on what they say.
